content: Bus bunching refers to two distinct phenomena. First, it describes a bus route characterized by highly irregular service intervals. Second, it represents a classical theoretical model that explains the cause of these irregular intervals. The theory posits that a bus running late tends to fall further behind schedule as it progresses along its route, while the bus following it tends to catch up, arriving earlier and earlier. The theory suggests that eventually, the two buses form a pair, traveling one right after the other. This pairing disrupts the intended service intervals, leading to a breakdown in the regularity of the schedule. When buses are stuck together in this manner, they are referred to as a bus bunch or banana bus. This phenomenon can involve more than two buses and has been hypothesized as a primary cause of reliability issues in bus and metro systems. Causes of Bus Bunching Abnormal Passenger Loads The time required for a bus to complete its route is directly influenced by the number of passengers boarding or alighting at stops. A bus that is already running late tends to attract more passengers due to the longer gap in service since the previous bus. This increased passenger load further delays the late bus, exacerbating the problem. Speed of Individual Drivers Another contributing factor is the variability in driving speeds among bus operators. Some drivers are faster than others, which can lead to buses catching up with one another, particularly on long or high-frequency routes. Deliberate Actions by Drivers According to an article by Lyndsey Layton titled Progress Has Passed Metrobus (December 27, 2005), bus bunching may sometimes be intentionally caused by drivers. In such cases, a driver may deliberately slow down, allowing the bus ahead to pick up more passengers, thereby reducing their own workload. Practical Observations and Challenges Despite the theoretical basis for bus bunching, data from vehicle tracking systems has not consistently supported its existence as a major cause of irregular service intervals. Studies of metro operations have largely debunked the idea that pairwise bus bunching is a significant factor in service irregularities. Instead, these studies have attributed irregularities to other issues in scheduling and operational processes. Recent research has shown that simulation models based on the classical theory of bus bunching fail to replicate real-world conditions as recorded in bus location tracking databases. Even when random external events are incorporated into these models, they do not accurately reflect actual service intervals. One researcher attributed the persistence of the classical theory to physics envy, suggesting that the theory's appeal lies in its resemblance to physical systems rather than its practical applicability. While station dwell time does influence variability in service intervals, other explanations for bus service unreliability include: Inability to Reset Scheduled Departure Times: At the start of a route, it is often difficult to reset departure times due to the remote and isolated nature of outer terminals in bus networks. Supervisors are rarely stationed at these terminals because it is uneconomical to do so for a single route. However, some transit systems have successfully used AVL/CAD (Automatic Vehicle Location/Computer-Aided Dispatch) systems to remotely adjust terminal departure times, improving overall service regularity. Inadequate Recovery Margins in Schedules: Schedules that provide minimal recovery time relative to actual running time performance tend to accumulate delays. Service control actions, such as unscheduled short-turning, are often employed to keep drivers within union-agreed contractual work parameters. However, unscheduled short-turning frequently occurs during off-peak periods, forcing many passengers to transfer to the next bus, which may already be crowded. Street Closures and Traffic Conditions: Bus routes are often affected by street closures, which increase running times and contribute to further delays. This necessitates greater intervention to ensure drivers remain within their work parameters. Driver Aggressiveness: The driving style of individual operators also impacts bus operations. Research on the Portland, Oregon bus network has quantified the effect of driver aggressiveness on service variability. Chaos Theory and Bus Bunching Bus bunching is an example of chaos theory in action. The orderly progression of buses along a route is inherently unstable, and without intervention, buses naturally tend to form bunches. However, it is impossible to predict in advance which buses will bunch and which will maintain their schedule. This unpredictability arises from random external factors such as traffic conditions, stoplights, and the number of passengers at each stop.
